AcceptStaffInvitationRequest.description:
Deliberately has no `staff_level` and no `access_until`.

The tier and the window come from the invitation row. A field here would be
the person being granted access choosing their own authority, which is the
whole vulnerability this flow exists to avoid - and one that a well-meaning
"let the client send what the preview returned" would introduce silently.
AcceptStaffInvitationRequest.title: AcceptStaffInvitationRequest

AgentBlueprint.description: The generated configuration, before it becomes an agent.
AgentBlueprint.title: AgentBlueprint

description.description: What the business does, who it serves, and what the agent should do.
description.title: Description

website_url.description: Optional. Read to match tone and seed the knowledge base.
website_url.title: Website Url

AgentUpdate.description:
Every field optional - PATCH semantics. Only keys present in the request
body are applied, so a client can update one field without needing to
round-trip the whole object and risk clobbering a concurrent edit.
AgentUpdate.title: AgentUpdate

AllocationUpdate.description:
A ceiling on the agency's pool for one client workspace.

`null` means "draw freely" - not zero. The two are genuinely different and
the difference is somebody's agent answering or not, so the field is
nullable rather than defaulting to a number.
AllocationUpdate.title: AllocationUpdate

AssistantEscalation.description:
Turning a chat into a ticket. Everything is optional and pre-filled.

The subject and body default to what the assistant already built from the
transcript, so the common case is one button with nothing to type.
AssistantEscalation.title: AssistantEscalation

BillingProfileIn.description: The addressee for receipts, and the tax registration to print on them.
BillingProfileIn.title: BillingProfileIn

file.description: A chat archive exported from here
file.title: File

BulkConversationUpdate.description:
A batch action over conversations the caller already has ids for.

Capped at 200. That is comfortably inside a request at today's row sizes,
and the point where it would not be is the point where the right answer is
a queued job rather than a longer timeout - so the cap is a design decision
rather than a guess, and it fails loudly instead of timing out.
BulkConversationUpdate.title: BulkConversationUpdate

BulkOutcome.description:
One item's result inside a bulk response.

A bulk endpoint that returns `200 OK` after partially failing is worse than
one that does not exist, because the operator believes it worked and finds
out later from a customer. Every item reports for itself.
BulkOutcome.title: BulkOutcome

Category.description: A kind of lifecycle email, and the unit a person can turn off.
Category.title: Category

ChangePlanRequest.description: The plan an existing subscriber moves to. Price and product are ours.
ChangePlanRequest.title: ChangePlanRequest

CheckoutRequest.description: What to buy. Notably absent: any price, and any product id.

tier.description: One of the purchasable tiers, or 'topup'
tier.title: Tier

CheckoutRequest.title: CheckoutRequest

ContactFieldDef.description: A field the model extracts from free conversation.
ContactFieldDef.title: ContactFieldDef

DarkPalette.description:
The second palette, used when the *visitor's* system is set to dark.

Not the tenant's preference - the visitor's. A tenant previewing on a light
laptop is not the person the choice is for, and a widget that stays bright
white on a dark site reads as broken rather than as branded.

Every field is optional. A tenant who sets none gets a palette derived from
their light one at render time, which is a better default than forcing them
through a second colour picker they did not ask for.
DarkPalette.title: DarkPalette

DelegationUpdate.description:
What a client workspace may do inside itself.

Exactly one of `preset` or `capabilities`. A preset is what almost everyone
wants; the list is for the agency with a specific arrangement.
DelegationUpdate.title: DelegationUpdate

DirectoryConfig.description:
Generic routing table: category + choice resolves to a link.

Replaces the previous hard-coded `doctors_config`. A clinic reads it as
branch/doctor/appointment link, a dealership as city/showroom/booking link,
a university as campus/department/enquiry form - same code, no per-vertical
branches.
DirectoryConfig.title: DirectoryConfig

DocumentDownload.description:
A signed link to a stored original.

`expires_in` is returned so a client can decide whether to reuse the URL or
ask for a fresh one. Presigned links are bearer credentials - anybody who
has the string has the file until it lapses - so they are deliberately
short-lived and re-issued per click rather than cached in a page.
DocumentDownload.title: DocumentDownload

DocumentStatusRead.description: Polled after upload until the document reaches a terminal state.
DocumentStatusRead.title: DocumentStatusRead

EmailOnlyRequest.description:
Shared by forgot-password, resend-verification and otp/request.

All three answer identically whether or not the address exists, so they take
identical input and return identical output. Giving them one schema makes
that symmetry visible rather than something three handlers happen to agree
on.
EmailOnlyRequest.title: EmailOnlyRequest

EventDescriptor.description:
One entry in the catalogue.

The catalogue exists because a subscription list is otherwise a guessing
game: a customer picking events from an enum in our source is a customer
reading our source.
EventDescriptor.title: EventDescriptor

GoogleStartResponse.description:
What the browser needs to begin the flow.

`state`, `nonce` and `code_verifier` are generated server-side for the
entropy, then handed back for the SPA to keep in `sessionStorage` and return
with the code. Holding them here instead would mean issuing a session to
somebody who does not have one yet - a cookie and a cleanup job, to save one
round trip.
GoogleStartResponse.title: GoogleStartResponse

Gradient.description: A two-stop linear gradient for the launcher and header.
Gradient.title: Gradient

GreetingTranslation.description: The greeting and suggested questions, in one other language.
GreetingTranslation.title: GreetingTranslation

HierarchyNode.description:
One workspace in the tree. Recursive - a client may run clients of its
own, up to the depth the database enforces.
HierarchyNode.title: HierarchyNode

InvitationPreview.description:
What the acceptance page may know before anyone has signed in.

Deliberately thin. Holding the token earns the workspace's name - enough to
answer "join what?" - and nothing else: no member list, no agents, no counts.
InvitationPreview.title: InvitationPreview

LanguageConfig.description:
How an agent handles more than one language. Defaults are the
behaviour of an agent that never opened the settings: follow the page,
follow the visitor, every language, greetings translated automatically.
LanguageConfig.title: LanguageConfig

Message.description: Simple acknowledgement for endpoints with nothing else to return.
Message.title: Message

MfaChallengeResponse.description:
What `/login` returns when the account has a second factor.

A distinct shape from `TokenResponse` rather than a `TokenResponse` with
empty tokens, so a client cannot accidentally treat an unfinished sign-in
as a finished one. `mfa_required` is the discriminator; a client that has
never heard of MFA sees no `access_token` and fails loudly rather than
proceeding half-authenticated.
MfaChallengeResponse.title: MfaChallengeResponse

MfaCodesResponse.description: Recovery codes. Shown once; only digests are stored.
MfaCodesResponse.title: MfaCodesResponse

MfaDisableRequest.description:
Turning it off needs both factors, not one.

The password, because an unlocked session should not be able to remove the
control that protects the account - that is the exact scenario a second
factor exists for. And a current code, because otherwise a stolen session
plus a known password strips it, which is the combination MFA is meant to
survive.
MfaDisableRequest.title: MfaDisableRequest

MfaSetupResponse.description: Everything needed to enrol, returned exactly once.
MfaSetupResponse.title: MfaSetupResponse

OrgRole.description:
Role of a user within one organization.

`owner` is the billing contact and the only role that can delete the
organization or transfer ownership; there is always at least one.
`viewer` is read-only, which is what a client stakeholder gets when they
want to watch conversation volume without being able to change a prompt.
OrgRole.title: OrgRole

PlaygroundOverrides.description: The behaviour fields a test may try. Bounds match `AgentUpdate`.
PlaygroundOverrides.title: PlaygroundOverrides

PolicyPatch.description:
A settings change on an existing channel.

Every field is optional and only the ones actually SENT are applied, so
`null` means "clear this" - drop the quiet window, remove the cap, unscope
from an agent - rather than "leave it alone". `model_fields_set` is what
carries that distinction, which is why this cannot simply reuse
`PolicyRequest` with defaults.

`channel` and `destination` are absent on purpose: they identify the row,
and a new destination is a new channel that has to be verified before
anything is sent to it.
PolicyPatch.title: PolicyPatch

ProactiveTrigger.description:
A rule for opening the conversation before the visitor does.

Evaluated entirely in the browser. A server round trip per trigger would
multiply the highest-volume request in the system by every page view on
every customer site, to answer a question the client can already answer.

Validated here anyway, because a rule that fires on every scroll event is a
configuration a tenant should not be able to save - the cost of that
mistake lands on their visitors and on our quota, and neither of them gets
a say.
ProactiveTrigger.title: ProactiveTrigger

SavedViewCreate.description:
A named filter set.

`filters` is free-form here and validated against the target resource's
allow-list in the service - see `views_service.validate`. Declaring the
shape in this schema instead would mean one model per resource and a new
one every time a list gains a filter; validating against the endpoint's own
vocabulary keeps the two in step by construction.
SavedViewCreate.title: SavedViewCreate

website_url.description: A website address, with or without a scheme.
website_url.title: Website Url

SearchRequest.description:
Exposed so a tenant can see exactly what their agent retrieves for a
question - the fastest way to diagnose a bad answer.
SearchRequest.title: SearchRequest

StaffInvitationPreview.description:
What the staff acceptance page may know before anyone has signed in.

Thinner than its workspace counterpart, and for a sharper reason: this token
is an offer of access to every customer's data, so holding it earns the
recipient the terms of the offer - the tier, the end date, who made it - and
nothing whatsoever about the platform or its customers.

`needs_password` is what lets the page ask for one only when it is wanted:
true for an address with no account, and for one that has only ever signed
in with Google and therefore has no password to sign into the console with.
StaffInvitationPreview.title: StaffInvitationPreview

What the customer surfaces need to draw the banner that says so - whose
workspace, whether changes are allowed, and when it ends by itself.

Every field optional; only what is sent is changed.

Not a subclass of `ToolBase`, because the cross-field rules there need the
whole record to be present. A partial update is merged onto the stored row
and then re-validated as a whole - see `service.update_tool`.

WebhookCreate.description:
Note what is absent: a secret.

It is generated here, from `secrets.token_urlsafe`, rather than accepted
from the caller. A tenant-chosen signing key is a tenant-chosen *weak*
signing key eventually, and there is no reason to offer the choice - the
receiver has to store whatever it is told either way.

WebhookCreated.description:
The creation response, and the only one that carries the secret.

A separate model rather than an optional field on `WebhookResponse`, so
that returning the secret is something a route has to *choose* by naming
this type. An optional field is one careless `response_model` away from
appearing on a list endpoint.

WidgetTheme.description:
Widget appearance. Extra keys are kept so the dashboard can add controls
without a migration; the widget ignores what it does not recognise.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Contrast is enforced, and enforced differently for the two callers
--------------------------------------------------------------------

A tenant editing colours by hand is **rejected**, with the measured ratio
and a hex that would pass, because they can see the result and are entitled
to choose which colour moves.

A theme produced by the one-prompt generator is **repaired** before it
reaches this class - see `generation_service._readable_theme`. Failing an
entire agent generation because a model picked a hex nobody asked for, and
which the customer will never see, would be an absurd way to lose a signup.

Two policies, one definition of readable, which is why the definition lives
in `app.platform.contrast` and not here.
WidgetTheme.title: WidgetTheme

info.description:
The Integrable Cloud API.

Authenticate with `Authorization: Bearer sk_live_...`. Keys are created in the agent studio under Developer -> API keys and carry scopes; a call outside a key's scopes is refused with 403.

Every mutating request accepts `Idempotency-Key`. Every response carries `X-API-Version` and, where a budget applies, `RateLimit-*`.

There is also an MCP server at `/mcp` for connecting this workspace to Claude, ChatGPT or an editor. It uses the same API keys.
info.title: integrable.cloud

get.description:
What has been happening in this workspace, by event.

Reads `event_rollup_daily`, which a handler has been maintaining since the
event ledger shipped and which no query had ever touched. One indexed
upsert per dispatched event had been paying for a table nobody read.

Labelled in plain language rather than by event name. An activity feed that
says `conversation.answer_refused` is a log file with a web page in front
of it; one that says "Could not answer a question" is the panel a business
owner scans on a Monday.

post.description:
Builds a fully-configured agent from one plain-language description.

This is the product's main path, not a convenience wrapper: the customer
describes their business, and everything the advanced screens expose -
persona, greeting, starter questions, which details to collect and when,
what to extract from conversation, routing, theme - is inferred. They open
the advanced screens only to disagree with something.

With `import_website`, the site is also crawled into the knowledge base in
the background, so the agent can answer real questions from its first minute
rather than being an empty persona.

get.description:
Models this org's plan may select, with measured characteristics.

Shaped for a model switcher rather than for a developer. The owner sees the
lab that made it and one word for what it is good at - `name` is
"Alibaba - Long memory", not `qwen/qwen3.7-flash` - because a model id is
meaningless to the person choosing and mildly alarming to the rest.

`ttft_ms` is the number worth putting next to the choice, and it is ours:
OpenRouter publishes no latency at all (its `latency_last_30m` returns null
on every endpoint), so every figure here came from
`scripts/model_probe.py` running one real support turn against our own
host. `measured_on` ships with it, because a latency claim with no date is
marketing rather than measurement.

get.description:
The preset picker's contents, and which of them this plan can use.

Registered above `/{agent_id}` because FastAPI matches in declaration
order and `widget` would otherwise be read as an agent id.

The locked ones are returned, not filtered out. A picker that hides what
the plan does not include cannot sell it, and the whole commercial case
for the premium half of this catalogue is that somebody looks at it. Each
row carries its tier; `required_plan` says what the cheapest plan that
unlocks them is, so the lock can name a price instead of saying no.

get.description:
Downloads recent conversations as a portable, verifiable bundle.

The file is self-describing JSON with a checksum and a signature, so it
can be kept, mailed to somebody, and brought back later to be looked at -
including by a customer who has cancelled, which is a promise worth making
and cheap to keep.

`redact=true` strips names, emails, phone numbers and the visitor id while
keeping every transcript and every number derived from them. It exists
because the most common reason to export chats is to send them to
somebody, and the second most common regret is having sent personal data
with them.

get.description:
One page of conversations.

`cursor` is the mode to use for anything that walks the whole list -
exports, infinite scroll, an integration syncing conversations. It is
constant-cost at any depth and stable while new conversations arrive;
`page` is neither, and exists because a numbered pager needs it.

`search_transcript=true` widens `q` from metadata - visitor, page, contact
details, title - to what was actually *said*, using the full-text index
that has been in the schema since the first migration and, until now, was
referenced by no query in the codebase.

`count=false` skips the `COUNT(*)`, which is the half of the request that
scans. `total` comes back as -1 and `has_more` is the field to read.

`outcome`, `sentiment`, `intent`, `min_rating` / `max_rating`,
`min_lead_score` and the date bounds are what make the insight panels
lead somewhere. Before them, the dashboard could tell a customer that 22%
of their pricing conversations were refused and offer no way to open those
twelve conversations - which is a report, not a tool.

right answer is a job, not a longer timeout.

get.description:
The snippet a customer pastes, in two forms.

`snippet` is the one almost everybody wants: a stable URL that picks up
every widget improvement without them touching their HTML again.

`pinned_snippet` is for the customer whose change-control process forbids a
third-party script that can change under them - which is most enterprises,
and the question arrives during a security review rather than during a
trial. It names the content-hashed build and carries an `integrity` hash,
so the browser refuses to execute anything but the exact bytes that were
reviewed.

Pinning is offered, never defaulted. A pinned embed stops receiving fixes,
including security ones, until somebody edits their page - so it has to be
a decision the customer makes rather than one we make for them.

get.description:
A short-lived signed link to the file the customer originally uploaded.

Returns the URL rather than the bytes. Proxying a download through the API
holds a worker for as long as somebody's connection lasts, which is a poor
use of a small container when the object store does this natively - and the
signature is what enforces the tenant boundary, not the redirect.

404 rather than 204 when no original exists, because "this document has no
stored source" and "no such document" are the same answer to a caller: there
is nothing here to download. Documents added as pasted text or crawled URLs
never had a source file, and documents uploaded before this shipped were not
kept.

post.description:
Uploads the agent's avatar and points the theme at it.

`widget_theme.avatar_url` has been settable since themes existed, with
nothing behind it - a tenant could name an image they hosted themselves and
had no way to supply one otherwise. Object storage removed that blocker on
2026-08-29; this is the endpoint that was left.

The size cap is enforced *while reading*, as it is on document upload and
for the same reason: `await file.read()` on an unbounded body buffers the
whole thing before any check runs, so one large request can exhaust the
container before the limit is consulted.

The file's type is read from its bytes, never from the `Content-Type` the
uploader claims - see `app.platform.images`. The stored object is served to
every visitor of the tenant's website, and an attacker-chosen type there is
how an avatar becomes `text/html` on our own origin.

A palette from a sentence, or from the customer's own website.

Returns the theme without saving it unless `apply` is set. A colour scheme
is the most visible thing about a widget and the cheapest to disagree with,
so the default is to propose rather than to change - the tenant sees it in

rejected. Failing this request because a model chose a slightly too-light

picked; correcting it and telling them what changed is the useful version
of the same rule. See `theme_service.readable_theme`.

post.description:
Reads a bundle back and returns it as a viewable report.

**Writes nothing.** It parses, verifies the checksum and signature, and
returns a rendered view. That is what makes accepting a file from a user
safe at all: the worst a tampered bundle can do is render its own contents
back to whoever uploaded it, which is what a file viewer does by
definition.

Verification failures are reported specifically - "not from this product",
"edited since export", "from a different installation" are genuinely
different problems with different answers, and collapsing them into
"invalid file" wastes the customer's time.

clicking a link. That does put the token in browser history and in any

days, and why the page should exchange it for a session promptly.

Turns the second factor off. Needs the password *and* a current code.

Both, because either one alone defeats the point. A session that could
remove MFA with a password is a session in which a stolen password is still

whose phone is at the bottom of a canal has to be able to turn this off,
and they have already proved the password.

ten needs to know now rather than at zero.

post.description:
Exchanges a refresh token for a new pair.

Rotates: the presented token is spent, and presenting it again revokes the
whole session family - unless it is the same browser a few seconds later,
which is two tabs rather than a thief. See auth_service for both rules.

The session stays in the workspace its token family carries, so a switch
made an hour ago is still in force.

While a staff support session is open in this browser (`ic_support`), the
customer surfaces get a token for *that* workspace instead - see
`_support_token_response`. The refresh cookie is not rotated then.

post.description:
Moves this session into another workspace.

Any workspace the user is a member of, or one beneath it - an agency
entering a client's workspace acts there with the role it holds above.
Returns a token pair for the new workspace and rotates the refresh cookie
into it, so the switch survives every later refresh.

Needs both credentials: the access token says who is asking, the refresh
cookie is what gets moved. A stolen access token alone cannot mint a
long-lived session this way.

404 rather than 403 for a workspace the user cannot enter, so the endpoint
does not confirm which workspace ids exist.

post.description:
Moves an existing subscription to another plan, prorated, in place.

Answers with one of two things for the browser to do:

  `payment_link`   the bank wants the customer to authorise the charge -
                   send the browser there; the plan changes when the
                   provider's webhook reports the payment
  `pending`        the provider accepted it; the plan changes when its
                   `subscription.plan_changed` webhook lands, usually in
                   seconds, so the screen watches the subscription

The tier is NEVER changed here. A declined proration charge keeps the old
plan (`on_payment_failure: prevent_change`), and only the webhook knows
which way it went.

post.description:
Fires a synthetic event down the real delivery path.

Returns as soon as the delivery is queued - `202`-shaped behaviour with a
`200`, because the result is a row the caller then polls for rather than
something this request can wait on. Posting inline would be faster and
would skip the queue, the retry classification and the failure accounting,
so a test could pass on an endpoint every real delivery fails against.

The payload carries `"test": true` at the top level. A test event that a
receiver cannot distinguish from a real one is a test that creates a real
record in somebody's CRM.

put.description:
Turns tenant-scoped encryption on or off.

Both directions are safe and neither is instant.

**On** takes effect immediately for new writes once a key exists, and the
`crypto.seal_backlog` sweep converts what came before. Nothing becomes
unreadable in the meantime: a plaintext value opens as itself.

**Off** stops new writes being sealed and leaves existing ciphertext
sealed, which keeps reading correctly because the key is still there. It
does not decrypt anything, and saying otherwise would be the dangerous
lie - a customer who switches off, exports, and deletes their workspace
would otherwise expect plaintext they never got.
